title: Map an ordinary reaction and try an earlier response

sections.title: Understand the distinction
sections.body: A reaction chain includes event, interpretation, body cue, urge, action and consequence. The earliest usable cue is one actually noticed before action, not an earlier signal imagined afterward.

sections.title: Complete fictional practice material
sections.body: Fictional first request:09:00 message asks for help;09:00:05 Jo thinks “I must answer yes”;09:00:08 hand tightens;09:00:12 Jo agrees;09:05 calendar reveals a conflict. Second ordinary request:11:00 message;11:00:06 same thought;11:00:09 Jo notices grip;11:00:12 says “I will check and answer by noon”;11:03 calendar shows no free hour. No emergency or threatening relationship is involved.

sections.title: Work through the supplied case
sections.body: Map both sequences and choose an early response supported by actual noticing. State what changed and what remains uncertain before reading the outcome.

sections.title: Try a different case before checking
sections.body: A person notices tension only after saying yes. Can that occasion demonstrate an earlier pause?

checks.title: Compare reasoning and review the supplied result
checks.body: The noticed grip at 11:00:09 precedes the holding reply and can cue checking. Later fiction: Jo declines the unavailable hour at 11:10; no reaction from the requester is supplied. The first agreement still needs appropriate repair. Partial: report only the bodily cue. Incorrect: call the thought a proven cause or claim a changed relationship. Rehearsal alone remains preparation.
criteria: Timelines determine what was actually available
An earlier response fits a real noticed cue
Consequences and causal limits remain explicit

checks.title: Check the changed case
checks.body: No. Record late noticing and the actual agreement. A later suitable opportunity may test the cue; do not backdate awareness to make the chain succeed.
